sections.h2: What should a Wrightsville-area seller know about Johnson County?
sections.html:
Johnson County has Wrightsville as its seat and was created from Washington, Laurens and Emanuel land by a bill dated December 11, 1858. The county's history page describes the setting as rural, with tree-lined streets in town and easy driving to Macon, Savannah, Augusta and Milledgeville. The 1895 courthouse, renovated in 1938 and again in 1995, is a listed National Register property and anchors an older downtown that appraises differently from the farmhouses outside town.

Two smaller places add wrinkles. Kite dates to the 1890s and keeps a museum in a former Masonic lodge. Adrian sits on the line with Emanuel County, and that boundary zigzags through town like a Z, so one street can contain neighbors who file in different counties. A parcel near Adrian should be matched to the right county before you call a tax office.

The county covers 303.02 square miles of land, about 30 residents per square mile at the 2020 count. Expect listings to be acreage, wooded tracts or a farmhouse past the pavement.

sections.h2: How do Johnson County's housing figures look next to its neighbors?
sections.html:
The middle home value in Johnson County is under half of Jones County's, and the poverty rate of 33.4% is the highest of the four counties in the Census comparison.

Between the 2010 and 2020 counts Johnson County lost 791 residents, and the 2025 estimate wins back only part of that. People 65 and older are 20.9% of the total, and 88.5% of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so few homes turn over. Zero permits in 2025 means no new construction to price against.

sections.h2: What does the Johnson County economy look like in Census data?
sections.html:
Census figures show a thin local economy. In 2023 the county had 123 employer establishments, 888 jobs and a payroll of $29,673 thousand, and total retail sales in 2022 came to $69,176 thousand, or $7,510 per person. Health care and social assistance brought in $17,999 thousand in 2022, and transportation and warehousing $10,333 thousand.

Only 43.4% of residents 16 and older are in the civilian labor force, mean travel to work is 28.1 minutes, and 8.4% of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree. About 83.0% of households have a broadband subscription, and 18.6% of residents under 65 lack health insurance. For a seller, the takeaway is that many buyers are local, many are older, and financing depends on small-balance loans or cash. Pricing a house near the county median of $94,900 attracts more inquiries than pricing it like a Macon-area home.

sections.h2: Which Johnson County desks answer which tax question?
sections.html:
Two tax offices share the building at 2484 West Elm Street, Wrightsville, ZIP 31096.

  • Tax Commissioner at (478) 864-2565 ext. 1: sends bills, takes payments, supplies payoff numbers and handles tag renewals. Open Monday to Friday, 8 to 4:30, with online payment on the tax commissioner site.
  • Tax Assessors at (478) 864-3325 ext. 2: set value, accept returns and exemption forms, and receive appeals. Parcel records are on qPublic.
  • Clerk of Superior Court, 2557 East Elm Street, (478) 864-3484: keeps recorded deeds.
  • Probate Court, (478) 864-3316: opens estates when a deceased owner's name is still on the title.

The county tax commissioner page carries one unusual item. Owners whose timber was damaged and cut after Hurricane Helene can get tax relief by completing the form on the Georgia Forestry Commission's site, adding the supporting papers the form names, and delivering it to the tax commissioner. If you are selling woodland, ask whether such a claim was filed for your parcel.

sections.h2: How does an assessment dispute work in Johnson County?
sections.html:
The assessors' notices show two figures, the fair market value set for January 1 and the 40% slice of it that is actually taxed. Anyone whose parcel was bought or changed must return it to the assessors between January 1 and April 1, and the county's page puts the price of skipping that at 10% of the unreported value plus interest.

To contest a figure, write to the Board of Assessors with a postmark inside 45 days of the notice mailing. State your route in that first letter: the Revenue Department lists an equalization board, a hearing officer or an arbitrator, and the county's page adds superior court. Ask the assessors for the state form.

Money paid in error can come back if you ask in writing within three years. A refund that stems from a won appeal is issued automatically.

sections.h2: Do Johnson County owners get a local homestead break?
sections.html:
Not a local one. The Revenue Department's page for this county says none were adopted, so the state's own exemptions are the only choice.

  • Eligibility rests on owning the house and living in it as your legal residence, with the assessors deciding.
  • A form arriving after April 1 waits for the following year.
  • Once approved, the exemption continues until you move, sell or switch types.
  • Business personal property is returned every April 1, changed or not.
  • Mobile homes need a location permit within 30 days of being set, then a yearly renewal from January 1 through April 1.

Business inventory can qualify for a freeport exemption where voters approved one, requested at the assessors' desk in the return window.

sections.h2: What is the Johnson County payment deadline?
sections.html:
The state's fallback deadline is December 20, but counties may substitute December 1, November 15 or installment billing. No date appears on the Johnson County information page, so phone (478) 864-2565 ext. 1 and ask.

Interest waits until 60 days after the postmark, and penalties may follow on late balances. Because the bill is addressed to the owner, a lender holding escrow may not get a copy, and heirs who inherit should update the mailing address in writing.

Sellers ask whether a spring closing shifts the bill. It does not: the owner on January 1 carries that year's tax, and the state refunds nothing for a mid-year move, so the purchase contract has to divide it.

sections.h2: What if the Johnson County house I want to sell has unpaid tax?
sections.html:
Get the payoff in writing from the commissioner, then search the Clerk of Superior Court's docket for a recorded lien. Parcels that stay delinquent can reach the sales listed on the commissioner's tax sales page.

The closing agent sends the payoff out of the seller's proceeds, and the lien is released as the deed records. Inherited houses need Probate Court first. A buyer paying cash and taking the home as-is can absorb repairs, but the payoff, the recorded deed and any estate paperwork still happen.

faqs.q: Who sends the Johnson County tax bill?
faqs.a: The tax commissioner does, from 2484 West Elm Street in Wrightsville. Call (478) 864-2565 ext. 1. The bill combines county, school and state tax, while value questions go to the assessors at (478) 864-3325 ext. 2.

faqs.q: Does Johnson County add a local homestead exemption?
faqs.a: No local one exists, according to the Revenue Department. The statewide exemptions apply, and the application must reach the county by April 1.

faqs.q: What is the Johnson County appeal window?
faqs.a: Forty-five days from the mailing of the assessment notice. Send a written appeal to the Board of Assessors that names your chosen route.

faqs.q: What is a typical home worth in Johnson County?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau reports a median of $94,900 for owner-occupied homes in 2020-2024. Median gross rent is $647 a month.

faqs.q: Does a January closing move the year's tax to the buyer?
faqs.a: Not automatically. The owner on January 1 is liable for the year, so the contract and closing statement decide how buyer and seller share it.
